Review: The method is unusually systematic and closely aligned with the research question. It distinguishes the aggregate export from the data needed for inference, treats runs rather than time samples as independent units, and separates the causal effect of randomized coupling from the predictive role of correlation length. The blocked factorial design, preregistration, synchronized measurements, explicit spatial-fit rules, null-calibrated onset definition, censoring-aware analysis, and restrained claims about mediation and generalizability are substantial strengths.

Feedback: Several implementation details need to be fixed before the protocol is fully reproducible. Specify how the null signals will disrupt phase locking while preserving relevant temporal and spatial dependence, and validate that procedure against plausible drive-locked signals that are not time-crystalline. Clarify the signal, unit-level aggregation, and spectral power definition used for the subharmonic score; the phrase “power in the target bin” is ambiguous for finite windows and a measured, potentially varying drive frequency. Explain how phase coherence across units and cycles is calculated and how ordinary response at half the drive frequency is distinguished from robust temporal order.

The onset definition also needs a precise mapping between fixed-length, potentially overlapping spectral windows and non-overlapping persistence blocks, including how boundaries and missing or failed spatial fits affect onset and censoring. For the primary analysis, state how onset-time contrasts will be derived from the discrete-time survival model and how the two primary outcomes’ multiplicity adjustment will be applied. Simulation-based sample-size planning is appropriate, but should specify the target contrast and assumptions about condition-specific onset, censoring, day effects, and model fit.

Finally, the proposed 3-by-2 design supports estimation of the coupling contrast at the reference drive level, but the chosen drive levels and reference level should be justified and set before confirmatory data collection. The array is finite and anisotropic, so the fit range and boundary correction require validation; goodness-of-fit failure may be condition-dependent and should be reported as a limitation, not only as missing data. These are resolvable protocol details rather than fundamental weaknesses.

Rating (1-5): 4
